passage:
Looking back, the signs were small. Manjula started wearing full sleeves in the May heat and flinched when anyone touched her arm. She began giving away her sketchbooks, and one lunch she said, "It won't matter soon anyway."

I'm Elizabeth, and I didn't know the right words. So I just sat next to her on the back steps and asked, "Are you okay? Really?" She talked for a long time. I didn't argue or tell her she was being dramatic. I only listened.

Then I said, "I'm scared for you. Let's go to Ms Fernandes together, right now." Manjula went white. "You promised you wouldn't tell anyone." I said I was sorry, and I walked her to the counsellor's room anyway. Ms Fernandes called her mother that same afternoon.

Manjula didn't speak to me for eleven days. Then a text came: "I'm still mad. Thank you for not letting it go."

qa.q: What did Manjula start giving away?
qa.a: Manjula started giving away her sketchbooks.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Manjula said, "You promised you wouldn't tell anyone"?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt torn and frightened: sorry to break a promise, but more scared for Manjula's safety, which is why Elizabeth still walked with her to the counsellor.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen who notices signs like these in a friend?
qa.a: Stay calm and listen without judging, say plainly that you are worried, and go to a trusted adult such as a counsellor the same day, even if the friend is angry.

qa.q: How might Manjula have seen Elizabeth's choice at first, and later?
qa.a: At first Manjula felt betrayed because a promise was broken; days later Manjula could still be angry and also see it as care, as the text shows.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing signs of despair in a friend, listening without judging, and bringing in a trusted adult despite the friend's anger.

Counsellor's note, Class 11, Tuesday.

At 3:40 Rashmi knocked on my door, holding Lakshmi by the wrist. Lakshmi was crying and angry. "She had no right," Lakshmi said, and would not sit down.

Rashmi told me what she had noticed over two weeks: Lakshmi skipping meals, sleeping through breaks, and last night a message saying "nobody would notice if I wasn't here." Rashmi said she had sat with Lakshmi in the stairwell first and let her talk without arguing. Then she said she couldn't keep it secret. Rashmi's hands were shaking the whole time.

I thanked Rashmi and asked her to wait outside. I stayed with Lakshmi, listened, and told her she was not in trouble. I called Lakshmi's father at 4:15; he came to school within the hour, and we agreed on a follow-up session tomorrow morning. I will also check in with Rashmi, who is carrying a lot.

qa.a: The counsellor called Lakshmi's father at 4:15.

qa.a: Rashmi was frightened and anxious, both for Lakshmi and about losing the friendship, yet chose to speak up anyway.

qa.a: Rashmi listened first without arguing, then refused to keep a dangerous secret and brought Lakshmi to a trusted adult the same day, so help started at once.

I live in the flat below Nikita's family, so I hear more than I should. Most nights this month there have been raised voices through the ceiling: the shop, the rent, a relative who hasn't paid back what he owes. Then a door bangs.

Nikita has started sitting on the stairs between our floors with earphones in. Once I sat nearby and noticed nothing was playing. Nikita kept picking at a thread on one sleeve and jumped at every sound from upstairs.

Nikita cried a little, then ate three biscuits. Now Nikita knocks on our door most evenings, just to talk.

Monday. Joseph's parents argued again after dinner about the bakery closing early for good. Joseph shut his bedroom door, turned his lamp off and lay awake. His maths homework stayed blank the next morning.

Thursday. His aunt Kalyani picked him up from football and bought two cups of sugarcane juice. "You've gone quiet," she said, and waited. Joseph finally said, "If they didn't have to pay my fees, they wouldn't fight." Kalyani shook her head. "Your parents are worried about work. That is theirs to carry, not yours. You are allowed to be scared, and you can tell me anytime."

Two weeks later. The arguments still happen, though less loudly. One evening Joseph said to his mother, "When you both shout, I feel scared." She sat down beside him and said sorry. Now, when things get tense, his parents take their talk out to the balcony, and Joseph finishes his homework at the kitchen table.

The print shop near the Rajgarh bus stand smelled of ink and hot paper. Preeti had been working there for four months when Urmila, the owner, called her to the counter and laid out three wedding cards.

"Two spelling mistakes in the groom's family name, and the date on this one is in the wrong font," Urmila said. "The family noticed before I did."

Preeti's face went hot. She wanted to say the file had come late. Instead she took a pen. "Can you show me where exactly? And do you check names in a certain order?"

Urmila showed her: names first, then dates, then venue, reading the card aloud slowly. Preeti wrote it down. "Thank you, Didi. I'll do it that way."

By Saturday Preeti had taped a small checklist beside the computer. When the next batch of cards went out without a single error, Urmila tapped the list and said nothing, but she smiled.

On Wednesday, in a small lab in Porto, Elif handed Beatriz back her weekly report with red lines through half a page.

"The data is good," Elif said. "But I read it three times and still couldn't find the result. A manager shouldn't have to hunt."

Beatriz felt the sting in her chest. She had stayed late on that report. She took a breath. "Could you show me one paragraph that works and one that doesn't? And where should the result go?"

Elif pulled up an older report by another technician. "Result first, in two sentences. Method after."

"That helps. Thank you," Beatriz said, and meant it more than she expected.

On Friday she sent the next report with a short summary at the top and the charts labelled. Elif replied within ten minutes: "This is exactly it. I'll share it as the example." Beatriz saved that message in a folder she called 'what worked'.

Today Binita stopped the stand-up and said, in front of all nine of us, "Saurabh, this dashboard is late again and the numbers don't match." Everyone looked at their shoes. My ears were burning. I said "noted" and nothing else.

So you want to know about my first real feedback? Okay. I'm Lokesh, and eight months ago I was a trainee at a small engineering firm.

Pankaj sir called me in and said my load calculation for a warehouse roof was wrong. And I just froze. Then I started saying sorry. Sorry, sorry, I'll redo it, sorry, I'll stay late. I think I said it nine times.

He waited and then said, "Lokesh, I don't need sorry. I need to know if you understand where the mistake is."

I didn't. So I finally asked, "Can you show me which step?" He pointed to the wind load. I asked two more questions, calm ones, and it made sense.

After that I started coming with questions instead of apologies. Last month he asked me to check someone else's calculation. That felt better than any sorry ever did.

Last Friday the head chef sent back Thomas's plate. "Sauce is split. Again." Thomas stood very still, then said, "Sorry, Chef, sorry, I'll redo it, sorry." He redid it too fast, and the second plate came back as well. I couldn't tell what he was thinking, but his hands were shaking a little.

I share the flat in Pune with Maria and Darshan, so I heard most of Sunday's fight from the kitchen.

It started with the laundry and grew fast. "You always leave everything for me," Maria said. Darshan snapped back, "And you never notice anything I do." Then it was about his mother, her job, last Diwali. Neither of them was talking about laundry anymore.

The job letter from Bengaluru sat on the table between them in the small Lucknow flat.

"Three years there, Wasim. It's the job I've wanted since college," Aparna said.

"And I've just started here. I can't move now." His voice rose, then he stopped. He reached across and put his hand over hers. "Sorry. I'm frustrated, not with you."

They didn't decide that night. But they went to bed holding hands.

passage:
Week one. Rajni announced she'd joined a weekend baking class. Jyoti rolled her eyes. "Oh wow, the great chef. Remember the burnt dal?" Their flatmate laughed; Rajni didn't. Later Rajni went to bed early without saying goodnight.

Week three. It had become a habit: sighs, little jokes about Rajni's "hobbies". Then Rajni said quietly, "When you roll your eyes at me, I feel small. I don't know how long I can live with that feeling." Jyoti opened her mouth to say "relax, it's a joke", and closed it. The words scared her.

Week six. Jyoti had started noticing her own eye-rolls before they happened. She'd begun saying one thing she liked each day, even when it felt awkward. That Saturday Rajni brought home a lopsided cake. Jyoti took a bite. "This is really good. You've learned a lot." Rajni looked at her a long moment, then smiled and cut her a bigger slice.

qa.q: What class did Rajni join?
qa.a: Rajni joined a weekend baking class.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when Rajni said she didn't know how long she could live with that feeling?
qa.a: Jyoti felt scared and ashamed, realising the jokes were hurting Rajni and could end the relationship.

qa.q: What did Jyoti change, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Jyoti caught her eye-rolls early and said one appreciative thing each day, replacing contempt with respect, which protects the relationship.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni when Jyoti mocks her hobbies?
qa.a: Rajni feels small and hurt, pulls away by going to bed early, and starts to doubt whether the relationship can last.

grounding: Shows how sarcasm and eye-rolling damage a relationship over weeks and how they are replaced by appreciation and respect.

passage:
Sit, Sahil. You're rolling your eyes at your wife a lot lately, and I know that look, because I wore it first.

When I was twenty-one and newly married to your Dada, I thought I was the clever one. He'd tell a story at dinner and I'd sigh, "Here we go again." When he tried to fix the radio, I'd laugh, "Genius at work." Everyone laughed. He stopped telling stories.

One evening I found him sitting outside alone. He said, "Jyoti, I feel like a joke in my own house." That sentence went through me like cold water. I saw that my little jokes had become a wall.

So I made myself notice what he did well: how patient he was with the neighbour's children, how neatly he kept accounts. I started saying it out loud. It took almost a year before the stories came back.

Your Dadi Jyoti learned that late. Learn it earlier than I did.

qa.q: What did Jyoti say when Dada tried to fix the radio?
qa.a: Jyoti laughed and said, "Genius at work."

qa.q: What did young Jyoti feel when Dada said he felt like a joke in his own house?
qa.a: Young Jyoti felt shocked and ashamed; the words went through her "like cold water" as she saw her jokes had become a wall.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did young Jyoti choose to do?
qa.a: Finding Dada alone outside and hearing how he felt; she chose to notice and say out loud what he did well, replacing mockery with appreciation.

qa.q: How might Dada have seen Jyoti differently once she started appreciating him?
qa.a: He likely felt respected and safe again, which is why, over about a year, he began telling stories at dinner once more.

grounding: Shows through an elder's memory how sarcasm and mockery harm a marriage and how appreciation and respect repair it.
